gene.name: complement C5a receptor 1
gene.function: Receptor for the chemotactic and inflammatory peptide anaphylatoxin C5a, stimulating chemotaxis, granule enzyme release, intracellular calcium release and superoxide anion production. Ligand binding causes a conformation change that triggers signaling via guanine nucleotide-binding proteins (G proteins) and modulates the activity of downstream effectors, such as adenylate cyclase. C5AR1 is coupled to G(i)/G(o) (GNAI1 or GNAO1) G alpha proteins and mediates inhibition of adenylate cyclase. The ligand interacts with at least two sites on the receptor: a high-affinity site on the extracellular N-terminus, and a second site in the transmembrane region which activates downstream signaling events.

gene.name: CF transmembrane conductance regulator
gene.function: Epithelial ion channel that plays an important role in the regulation of epithelial ion and water transport and fluid homeostasis. Mediates the transport of chloride ions across the cell membrane. Possesses an intrinsic ATPase activity and utilizes ATP to gate its channel; the passive flow of anions through the channel is gated by cycles of ATP binding and hydrolysis by the ATP-binding domains. The ion channel is also permeable to HCO(3)(-); selectivity depends on the extracellular chloride concentration. In vitro, mediates ATP-dependent glutathione flux. Exerts its function also by modulating the activity of other ion channels and transporters. Plays an important role in airway fluid homeostasis. Contributes to the regulation of the pH and the ion content of the airway surface fluid layer and thereby plays an important role in defense against pathogens. Modulates the activity of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) complex, in part by regulating the cell surface expression of the ENaC complex. Inhibits the activity of the ENaC channel containing subunits SCNN1A, SCNN1B and SCNN1G. Inhibits the activity of the ENaC channel containing subunits SCNN1D, SCNN1B and SCNN1G, but not of the ENaC channel containing subunits SCNN1A, SCNN1B and SCNN1G. May regulate bicarbonate secretion and salvage in epithelial cells by regulating the transporter SLC4A7. Can inhibit the chloride channel activity of ANO1. Plays a role in the chloride and bicarbonate homeostasis during sperm epididymal maturation and capacitation.

gene.name: chitinase 1
gene.function: Degrades chitin, chitotriose and chitobiose. May participate in the defense against nematodes and other pathogens. Isoform 3 has no enzymatic activity.

gene.name: crystallin alpha B
gene.function: May contribute to the transparency and refractive index of the lens. Has chaperone-like activity, preventing aggregation of various proteins under a wide range of stress conditions. In lens epithelial cells, stabilizes the ATP6V1A protein, preventing its degradation by the proteasome (By similarity). .

gene.name: cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily D member 6 (gene/pseudogene)
gene.function: A cytochrome P450 monooxygenase involved in the metabolism of fatty acids, steroids and retinoids. Mechanistically, uses molecular oxygen inserting one oxygen atom into a substrate, and reducing the second into a water molecule, with two electrons provided by NADPH via cytochrome P450 reductase (NADPH--hemoprotein reductase). Catalyzes the epoxidation of double bonds of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). Metabolizes endocannabinoid arachidonoylethanolamide (anandamide) to 20-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid ethanolamide (20-HETE-EA) and 8,9-, 11,12-, and 14,15-epoxyeicosatrienoic acid ethanolamides (EpETrE-EAs), potentially modulating endocannabinoid system signaling. Catalyzes the hydroxylation of carbon-hydrogen bonds. Metabolizes cholesterol toward 25- hydroxycholesterol, a physiological regulator of cellular cholesterol homeostasis. Catalyzes the oxidative transformations of all-trans retinol to all-trans retinal, a precursor for the active form all-trans-retinoic acid. Also involved in the oxidative metabolism of drugs such as antiarrhythmics, adrenoceptor antagonists, and tricyclic antidepressants.

gene.name: cytochrome P450 family 3 subfamily A member 4
gene.function: A cytochrome P450 monooxygenase involved in the metabolism of sterols, steroid hormones, retinoids and fatty acids. Mechanistically, uses molecular oxygen inserting one oxygen atom into a substrate, and reducing the second into a water molecule, with two electrons provided by NADPH via cytochrome P450 reductase (NADPH--hemoprotein reductase). Catalyzes the hydroxylation of carbon-hydrogen bonds. Exhibits high catalytic activity for the formation of hydroxyestrogens from estrone (E1) and 17beta- estradiol (E2), namely 2-hydroxy E1 and E2, as well as D-ring hydroxylated E1 and E2 at the C-16 position. Plays a role in the metabolism of androgens, particularly in oxidative deactivation of testosterone. Metabolizes testosterone to less biologically active 2beta- and 6beta- hydroxytestosterones. Contributes to the formation of hydroxycholesterols (oxysterols), particularly A-ring hydroxylated cholesterol at the C- 4beta position, and side chain hydroxylated cholesterol at the C-25 position, likely contributing to cholesterol degradation and bile acid biosynthesis. Catalyzes bisallylic hydroxylation of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). Catalyzes the epoxidation of double bonds of PUFA with a preference for the last double bond. Metabolizes endocannabinoid arachidonoylethanolamide (anandamide) to 8,9-, 11,12-, and 14,15- epoxyeicosatrienoic acid ethanolamides (EpETrE-EAs), potentially modulating endocannabinoid system signaling. Plays a role in the metabolism of retinoids. Displays high catalytic activity for oxidation of all-trans-retinol to all-trans-retinal, a rate- limiting step for the biosynthesis of all-trans-retinoic acid (atRA). Further metabolizes atRA toward 4-hydroxyretinoate and may play a role in hepatic atRA clearance. Responsible for oxidative metabolism of xenobiotics. Acts as a 2-exo- monooxygenase for plant lipid 1,8-cineole (eucalyptol). Metabolizes the majority of the administered drugs. Catalyzes sulfoxidation of the anthelmintics albendazole and fenbendazole. Hydroxylates antimalarial drug quinine. Acts as a 1,4-cineole 2-exo-monooxygenase. Also involved in vitamin D catabolism and calcium homeostasis. Catalyzes the inactivation of the active hormone calcitriol (1-alpha,25-dihydroxyvitamin D(3)).

gene.name: estrogen related receptor alpha
gene.function: Binds to an ERR-alpha response element (ERRE) containing a single consensus half-site, 5'-TNAAGGTCA-3'. Can bind to the medium- chain acyl coenzyme A dehydrogenase (MCAD) response element NRRE-1 and may act as an important regulator of MCAD promoter. Binds to the C1 region of the lactoferrin gene promoter. Requires dimerization and the coactivator, PGC-1A, for full activity. The ERRalpha/PGC1alpha complex is a regulator of energy metabolism. Induces the expression of PERM1 in the skeletal muscle.

gene.name: coagulation factor VII
gene.function: Initiates the extrinsic pathway of blood coagulation. Serine protease that circulates in the blood in a zymogen form. Factor VII is converted to factor VIIa by factor Xa, factor XIIa, factor IXa, or thrombin by minor proteolysis. In the presence of tissue factor and calcium ions, factor VIIa then converts factor X to factor Xa by limited proteolysis. Factor VIIa also converts factor IX to factor IXa in the presence of tissue factor and calcium. .

gene.name: glucosylceramidase beta 1
gene.function: Glucosylceramidase that catalyzes, within the lysosomal compartment, the hydrolysis of glucosylceramides/GlcCers (such as beta- D-glucosyl-(1<->1')-N-acylsphing-4-enine) into free ceramides (such as N-acylsphing-4-enine) and glucose. Plays a central role in the degradation of complex lipids and the turnover of cellular membranes. Through the production of ceramides, participates in the PKC-activated salvage pathway of ceramide formation. Catalyzes the glucosylation of cholesterol, through a transglucosylation reaction where glucose is transferred from GlcCer to cholesterol. GlcCer containing mono-unsaturated fatty acids (such as beta-D- glucosyl-N-(9Z-octadecenoyl)-sphing-4-enine) are preferred as glucose donors for cholesterol glucosylation when compared with GlcCer containing same chain length of saturated fatty acids (such as beta-D- glucosyl-N-octadecanoyl-sphing-4-enine). Under specific conditions, may alternatively catalyze the reverse reaction, transferring glucose from cholesteryl 3-beta-D-glucoside to ceramide (Probable). Can also hydrolyze cholesteryl 3-beta-D- glucoside producing glucose and cholesterol. Catalyzes the hydrolysis of galactosylceramides/GalCers (such as beta-D-galactosyl-(1<->1')-N- acylsphing-4-enine), as well as the transfer of galactose between GalCers and cholesterol in vitro, but with lower activity than with GlcCers. Contrary to GlcCer and GalCer, xylosylceramide/XylCer (such as beta-D-xyosyl-(1<->1')-N-acylsphing-4- enine) is not a good substrate for hydrolysis, however it is a good xylose donor for transxylosylation activity to form cholesteryl 3-beta- D-xyloside. Can also metabolize plant glycosyl phytosterols such as glucosylstigmasterol.

gene.name: glucosylceramidase beta 2
gene.function: Non-lysosomal glucosylceramidase that catalyzes the hydrolysis of glucosylceramides/GlcCers (such as beta-D-glucosyl- (1<->1')-N-acylsphing-4-enine) to free glucose and ceramides (such as N-acylsphing-4-enine). GlcCers are membrane glycosphingolipids that have a wide intracellular distribution (By similarity). They are the main precursors of more complex glycosphingolipids that play a role in cellular growth, differentiation, adhesion, signaling, cytoskeletal dynamics and membrane properties (By similarity). Involved in the transglucosylation of cholesterol, transfers glucose from GlcCer to cholesterol, thereby modifying its water solubility and biological properties. Under specific conditions, may catalyze the reverse reaction, transferring glucose from cholesteryl-3-beta-D- glucoside to ceramide (such as N-acylsphing-4-enine) (Probable). May play a role in the metabolism of bile acids. Able to hydrolyze bile acid 3-O- glucosides as well as to produce bile acid-glucose conjugates thanks to a bile acid glucosyl transferase activity. Catalyzes the hydrolysis of galactosylceramides/GalCers (such as beta-D-galactosyl-(1<->1')-N- acylsphing-4-enine), as well as the galactosyl transfer between GalCers and cholesterol in vitro with lower activity compared with their activity against GlcCers.

gene.name: GC vitamin D binding protein
gene.function: Involved in vitamin D transport and storage, scavenging of extracellular G-actin, enhancement of the chemotactic activity of C5 alpha for neutrophils in inflammation and macrophage activation. .

gene.name: gap junction protein beta 2
gene.function: Structural component of gap junctions. Gap junctions are dodecameric channels that connect the cytoplasm of adjoining cells. They are formed by the docking of two hexameric hemichannels, one from each cell membrane. Small molecules and ions diffuse from one cell to a neighboring cell via the central pore.

gene.name: galactosidase alpha
gene.function: Catalyzes the hydrolysis of glycosphingolipids and participates in their degradation in the lysosome. .

gene.name: hexosaminidase subunit beta
gene.function: Hydrolyzes the non-reducing end N-acetyl-D-hexosamine and/or sulfated N-acetyl-D-hexosamine of glycoconjugates, such as the oligosaccharide moieties from proteins and neutral glycolipids, or from certain mucopolysaccharides. The isozyme B does not hydrolyze each of these substrates, however hydrolyzes efficiently neutral oligosaccharide. Only the isozyme A is responsible for the degradation of GM2 gangliosides in the presence of GM2A. During fertilization is responsible, at least in part, for the zona block to polyspermy. Present in the cortical granules of non-activated oocytes, is exocytosed during the cortical reaction in response to oocyte activation and inactivates the sperm galactosyltransferase-binding site, accounting for the block in sperm binding to the zona pellucida (By similarity).

gene.name: heat shock protein family A (Hsp70) member 1A
gene.function: Molecular chaperone implicated in a wide variety of cellular processes, including protection of the proteome from stress, folding and transport of newly synthesized polypeptides, activation of proteolysis of misfolded proteins and the formation and dissociation of protein complexes. Plays a pivotal role in the protein quality control system, ensuring the correct folding of proteins, the re-folding of misfolded proteins and controlling the targeting of proteins for subsequent degradation. This is achieved through cycles of ATP binding, ATP hydrolysis and ADP release, mediated by co-chaperones. The co- chaperones have been shown to not only regulate different steps of the ATPase cycle, but they also have an individual specificity such that one co-chaperone may promote folding of a substrate while another may promote degradation. The affinity for polypeptides is regulated by its nucleotide bound state. In the ATP-bound form, it has a low affinity for substrate proteins. However, upon hydrolysis of the ATP to ADP, it undergoes a conformational change that increases its affinity for substrate proteins. It goes through repeated cycles of ATP hydrolysis and nucleotide exchange, which permits cycles of substrate binding and release. The co-chaperones are of three types: J-domain co-chaperones such as HSP40s (stimulate ATPase hydrolysis by HSP70), the nucleotide exchange factors (NEF) such as BAG1/2/3 (facilitate conversion of HSP70 from the ADP-bound to the ATP-bound state thereby promoting substrate release), and the TPR domain chaperones such as HOPX and STUB1. Maintains protein homeostasis during cellular stress through two opposing mechanisms: protein refolding and degradation. Its acetylation/deacetylation state determines whether it functions in protein refolding or protein degradation by controlling the competitive binding of co-chaperones HOPX and STUB1. During the early stress response, the acetylated form binds to HOPX which assists in chaperone-mediated protein refolding, thereafter, it is deacetylated and binds to ubiquitin ligase STUB1 that promotes ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation. Regulates centrosome integrity during mitosis, and is required for the maintenance of a functional mitotic centrosome that supports the assembly of a bipolar mitotic spindle. Enhances STUB1-mediated SMAD3 ubiquitination and degradation and facilitates STUB1-mediated inhibition of TGF-beta signaling. Essential for STUB1-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of FOXP3 in regulatory T-cells (Treg) during inflammation. Required as a co-chaperone for optimal STUB1/CHIP ubiquitination of NFATC3 (By similarity). Negatively regulates heat shock-induced HSF1 transcriptional activity during the attenuation and recovery phase period of the heat shock response. Involved in the clearance of misfolded PRDM1/Blimp-1 proteins. Sequesters them in the cytoplasm and promotes their association with SYNV1/HRD1, leading to proteasomal degradation.

gene.name: heat shock protein family A (Hsp70) member 5
gene.function: Endoplasmic reticulum chaperone that plays a key role in protein folding and quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen. Involved in the correct folding of proteins and degradation of misfolded proteins via its interaction with DNAJC10/ERdj5, probably to facilitate the release of DNAJC10/ERdj5 from its substrate (By similarity). Acts as a key repressor of the EIF2AK3/PERK and ERN1/IRE1- mediated unfolded protein response (UPR). In the unstressed endoplasmic reticulum, recruited by DNAJB9/ERdj4 to the luminal region of ERN1/IRE1, leading to disrupt the dimerization of ERN1/IRE1, thereby inactivating ERN1/IRE1 (By similarity). Also binds and inactivates EIF2AK3/PERK in unstressed cells. Accumulation of misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum causes release of HSPA5/BiP from ERN1/IRE1 and EIF2AK3/PERK, allowing their homodimerization and subsequent activation. Plays an auxiliary role in post-translational transport of small presecretory proteins across endoplasmic reticulum (ER). May function as an allosteric modulator for SEC61 channel-forming translocon complex, likely cooperating with SEC62 to enable the productive insertion of these precursors into SEC61 channel. Appears to specifically regulate translocation of precursors having inhibitory residues in their mature region that weaken channel gating. May also play a role in apoptosis and cell proliferation.

gene.name: interleukin 6
gene.function: Cytokine with a wide variety of biological functions in immunity, tissue regeneration, and metabolism. Binds to IL6R, then the complex associates to the signaling subunit IL6ST/gp130 to trigger the intracellular IL6-signaling pathway (Probable). The interaction with the membrane-bound IL6R and IL6ST stimulates 'classic signaling', whereas the binding of IL6 and soluble IL6R to IL6ST stimulates 'trans- signaling'. Alternatively, 'cluster signaling' occurs when membrane- bound IL6:IL6R complexes on transmitter cells activate IL6ST receptors on neighboring receiver cells (Probable). .

gene.name: lysosome associated membrane protein 1
gene.function: Lysosomal membrane glycoprotein which plays an important role in lysosome biogenesis, lysosomal pH regulation, autophagy and cholesterol homeostasis. Acts as an important regulator of lysosomal lumen pH regulation by acting as a direct inhibitor of the proton channel TMEM175, facilitating lysosomal acidification for optimal hydrolase activity. Also plays an important role in NK-cells cytotoxicity. Mechanistically, participates in cytotoxic granule movement to the cell surface and perforin trafficking to the lytic granule. In addition, protects NK-cells from degranulation-associated damage induced by their own cytotoxic granule content. Presents carbohydrate ligands to selectins.

gene.name: Parkinsonism associated deglycase
gene.function: Multifunctional protein with controversial molecular function which plays an important role in cell protection against oxidative stress and cell death acting as oxidative stress sensor and redox- sensitive chaperone and protease. It is involved in neuroprotective mechanisms like the stabilization of NFE2L2 and PINK1 proteins, male fertility as a positive regulator of androgen signaling pathway as well as cell growth and transformation through, for instance, the modulation of NF-kappa-B signaling pathway. Has been described as a protein and nucleotide deglycase that catalyzes the deglycation of the Maillard adducts formed between amino groups of proteins or nucleotides and reactive carbonyl groups of glyoxals. But this function is rebuted by other works. As a protein deglycase, repairs methylglyoxal- and glyoxal-glycated proteins, and releases repaired proteins and lactate or glycolate, respectively. Deglycates cysteine, arginine and lysine residues in proteins, and thus reactivates these proteins by reversing glycation by glyoxals. Acts on early glycation intermediates (hemithioacetals and aminocarbinols), preventing the formation of advanced glycation endproducts (AGE) that cause irreversible damage. Also functions as a nucleotide deglycase able to repair glycated guanine in the free nucleotide pool (GTP, GDP, GMP, dGTP) and in DNA and RNA. Is thus involved in a major nucleotide repair system named guanine glycation repair (GG repair), dedicated to reversing methylglyoxal and glyoxal damage via nucleotide sanitization and direct nucleic acid repair. Protects histones from adduction by methylglyoxal, controls the levels of methylglyoxal- derived argininine modifications on chromatin. Able to remove the glycations and restore histone 3, histone glycation disrupts both local and global chromatin architecture by altering histone-DNA interactions as well as histone acetylation and ubiquitination levels. Displays a very low glyoxalase activity that may reflect its deglycase activity. Eliminates hydrogen peroxide and protects cells against hydrogen peroxide-induced cell death. Required for correct mitochondrial morphology and function as well as for autophagy of dysfunctional mitochondria. Plays a role in regulating expression or stability of the mitochondrial uncoupling proteins SLC25A14 and SLC25A27 in dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta and attenuates the oxidative stress induced by calcium entry into the neurons via L-type channels during pacemaking. Regulates astrocyte inflammatory responses, may modulate lipid rafts-dependent endocytosis in astrocytes and neuronal cells. In pancreatic islets, involved in the maintenance of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and glucose homeostasis in an age- and diet dependent manner. Protects pancreatic beta cells from cell death induced by inflammatory and cytotoxic setting (By similarity). Binds to a number of mRNAs containing multiple copies of GG or CC motifs and partially inhibits their translation but dissociates following oxidative stress. Metal-binding protein able to bind copper as well as toxic mercury ions, enhances the cell protection mechanism against induced metal toxicity. In macrophages, interacts with the NADPH oxidase subunit NCF1 to direct NADPH oxidase-dependent ROS production, and protects against sepsis (By similarity).

gene.name: peroxiredoxin 2
gene.function: Thiol-specific peroxidase that catalyzes the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides to water and alcohols, respectively. Plays a role in cell protection against oxidative stress by detoxifying peroxides and as sensor of hydrogen peroxide-mediated signaling events. Might participate in the signaling cascades of growth factors and tumor necrosis factor-alpha by regulating the intracellular concentrations of H(2)O(2). .

gene.name: parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase
gene.function: Functions within a multiprotein E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, catalyzing the covalent attachment of ubiquitin moieties onto substrate proteins. Substrates include SYT11 and VDAC1. Other substrates are BCL2, CCNE1, GPR37, RHOT1/MIRO1, MFN1, MFN2, STUB1, SNCAIP, SEPTIN5, TOMM20, USP30, ZNF746, MIRO1 and AIMP2. Mediates monoubiquitination as well as 'Lys-6', 'Lys-11', 'Lys-48'-linked and 'Lys-63'-linked polyubiquitination of substrates depending on the context. Participates in the removal and/or detoxification of abnormally folded or damaged protein by mediating 'Lys-63'-linked polyubiquitination of misfolded proteins such as PARK7: 'Lys-63'-linked polyubiquitinated misfolded proteins are then recognized by HDAC6, leading to their recruitment to aggresomes, followed by degradation. Mediates 'Lys-63'-linked polyubiquitination of a 22 kDa O-linked glycosylated isoform of SNCAIP, possibly playing a role in Lewy-body formation. Mediates monoubiquitination of BCL2, thereby acting as a positive regulator of autophagy. Protects against mitochondrial dysfunction during cellular stress, by acting downstream of PINK1 to coordinate mitochondrial quality control mechanisms that remove and replace dysfunctional mitochondrial components. Depending on the severity of mitochondrial damage and/or dysfunction, activity ranges from preventing apoptosis and stimulating mitochondrial biogenesis to regulating mitochondrial dynamics and eliminating severely damaged mitochondria via mitophagy. Activation and recruitment onto the outer membrane of damaged/dysfunctional mitochondria (OMM) requires PINK1-mediated phosphorylation of both PRKN and ubiquitin. After mitochondrial damage, functions with PINK1 to mediate the decision between mitophagy or preventing apoptosis by inducing either the poly- or monoubiquitination of VDAC1, respectively; polyubiquitination of VDAC1 promotes mitophagy, while monoubiquitination of VDAC1 decreases mitochondrial calcium influx which ultimately inhibits apoptosis. When cellular stress results in irreversible mitochondrial damage, promotes the autophagic degradation of dysfunctional depolarized mitochondria (mitophagy) by promoting the ubiquitination of mitochondrial proteins such as TOMM20, RHOT1/MIRO1, MFN1 and USP30. Preferentially assembles 'Lys-6'-, 'Lys-11'- and 'Lys-63'-linked polyubiquitin chains, leading to mitophagy. The PINK1-PRKN pathway also promotes fission of damaged mitochondria by PINK1-mediated phosphorylation which promotes the PRKN-dependent degradation of mitochondrial proteins involved in fission such as MFN2. This prevents the refusion of unhealthy mitochondria with the mitochondrial network or initiates mitochondrial fragmentation facilitating their later engulfment by autophagosomes. Regulates motility of damaged mitochondria via the ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of MIRO1 and MIRO2; in motor neurons, this likely inhibits mitochondrial intracellular anterograde transport along the axons which probably increases the chance of the mitochondria undergoing mitophagy in the soma. Involved in mitochondrial biogenesis via the 'Lys-48'-linked polyubiquitination of transcriptional repressor ZNF746/PARIS which leads to its subsequent proteasomal degradation and allows activation of the transcription factor PPARGC1A. Limits the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Regulates cyclin-E during neuronal apoptosis. In collaboration with CHPF isoform 2, may enhance cell viability and protect cells from oxidative stress. Independently of its ubiquitin ligase activity, protects from apoptosis by the transcriptional repression of p53/TP53. May protect neurons against alpha synuclein toxicity, proteasomal dysfunction, GPR37 accumulation, and kainate-induced excitotoxicity. May play a role in controlling neurotransmitter trafficking at the presynaptic terminal and in calcium-dependent exocytosis. May represent a tumor suppressor gene.

gene.name: prosaposin
gene.function: Saposins are specific low-molecular mass non-enzymatic glycoproteins that act as activator proteins for lysosomal sphingolipid-degrading enzymes, facilitating the hydrolysis of sphingolipids by extracting lipid substrates from membranes and presenting them to their respective enzymes. They are derived from a common precursor protein, prosaposin, which is proteolytically cleaved to yield four homologous proteins (saposin A, B, C, and D), each with distinct but partially overlapping lipid and enzyme specificities. .

gene.name: S100 calcium binding protein A9
gene.function: S100A9 is a calcium- and zinc-binding protein which plays a prominent role in the regulation of inflammatory processes and immune response. It can induce neutrophil chemotaxis, adhesion, can increase the bactericidal activity of neutrophils by promoting phagocytosis via activation of SYK, PI3K/AKT, and ERK1/2 and can induce degranulation of neutrophils by a MAPK-dependent mechanism. Predominantly found as calprotectin (S100A8/A9) which has a wide plethora of intra- and extracellular functions. The intracellular functions include: facilitating leukocyte arachidonic acid trafficking and metabolism, modulation of the tubulin-dependent cytoskeleton during migration of phagocytes and activation of the neutrophilic NADPH-oxidase. Also participates in regulatory T-cell differentiation together with CD69. Activates NADPH-oxidase by facilitating the enzyme complex assembly at the cell membrane, transferring arachidonic acid, an essential cofactor, to the enzyme complex and S100A8 contributes to the enzyme assembly by directly binding to NCF2/P67PHOX. The extracellular functions involve pro-inflammatory, antimicrobial, oxidant-scavenging and apoptosis- inducing activities. Its pro- inflammatory activity includes recruitment of leukocytes, promotion of cytokine and chemokine production, and regulation of leukocyte adhesion and migration. Acts as an alarmin or a danger associated molecular pattern (DAMP) molecule and stimulates innate immune cells via binding to pattern recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) and receptor for advanced glycation endproducts (AGER). Binding to TLR4 and AGER activates the MAP-kinase and NF-kappa-B signaling pathways resulting in the amplification of the pro-inflammatory cascade. Has antimicrobial activity towards bacteria and fungi and exerts its antimicrobial activity probably via chelation of Zn(2+) which is essential for microbial growth. Can induce cell death via autophagy and apoptosis and this occurs through the cross-talk of mitochondria and lysosomes via reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the process involves BNIP3. Can regulate neutrophil number and apoptosis by an anti-apoptotic effect; regulates cell survival via ITGAM/ITGB and TLR4 and a signaling mechanism involving MEK-ERK. Its role as an oxidant scavenger has a protective role in preventing exaggerated tissue damage by scavenging oxidants. Can act as a potent amplifier of inflammation in autoimmunity as well as in cancer development and tumor spread. Has transnitrosylase activity; in oxidatively-modified low-densitity lipoprotein (LDL(ox))- induced S-nitrosylation of GAPDH on 'Cys-247' proposed to transfer the NO moiety from NOS2/iNOS to GAPDH via its own S-nitrosylated Cys-3. The iNOS-S100A8/A9 transnitrosylase complex is proposed to also direct selective inflammatory stimulus-dependent S- nitrosylation of multiple targets such as ANXA5, EZR, MSN and VIM by recognizing a [IL]-x-C-x-x-[DE] motif.

gene.name: scavenger receptor class B member 2
gene.function: Acts as a lysosomal receptor for glucosylceramidase (GBA1) targeting. .

gene.name: solute carrier family 6 member 3
gene.function: Mediates sodium- and chloride-dependent transport of dopamine. Also mediates sodium- and chloride-dependent transport of norepinephrine (also known as noradrenaline) (By similarity). Regulator of light-dependent retinal hyaloid vessel regression, downstream of OPN5 signaling (By similarity).

gene.name: sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 1
gene.function: Converts sphingomyelin to ceramide. Exists as two enzymatic forms that arise from alternative trafficking of a single protein precursor, one that is targeted to the endolysosomal compartment, whereas the other is released extracellularly. However, in response to various forms of stress, lysosomal exocytosis may represent a major source of the secretory form.

gene.name: synuclein alpha
gene.function: Neuronal protein that plays several roles in synaptic activity such as regulation of synaptic vesicle trafficking and subsequent neurotransmitter release. Participates as a monomer in synaptic vesicle exocytosis by enhancing vesicle priming, fusion and dilation of exocytotic fusion pores. Mechanistically, acts by increasing local Ca(2+) release from microdomains which is essential for the enhancement of ATP-induced exocytosis. Also acts as a molecular chaperone in its multimeric membrane-bound state, assisting in the folding of synaptic fusion components called SNAREs (Soluble NSF Attachment Protein REceptors) at presynaptic plasma membrane in conjunction with cysteine string protein-alpha/DNAJC5. This chaperone activity is important to sustain normal SNARE-complex assembly during aging. Also plays a role in the regulation of the dopamine neurotransmission by associating with the dopamine transporter (DAT1) and thereby modulating its activity.

gene.name: TBC1 domain family member 15
gene.function: Acts as a GTPase activating protein for RAB7A. Does not act on RAB4, RAB5 or RAB6 (By similarity). .

gene.name: transcription factor A, mitochondrial
gene.function: Binds to the mitochondrial light strand promoter and functions in mitochondrial transcription regulation. Component of the mitochondrial transcription initiation complex, composed at least of TFB2M, TFAM and POLRMT that is required for basal transcription of mitochondrial DNA. In this complex, TFAM recruits POLRMT to a specific promoter whereas TFB2M induces structural changes in POLRMT to enable promoter opening and trapping of the DNA non-template strand. Required for accurate and efficient promoter recognition by the mitochondrial RNA polymerase. Promotes transcription initiation from the HSP1 and the light strand promoter by binding immediately upstream of transcriptional start sites. Is able to unwind DNA. Bends the mitochondrial light strand promoter DNA into a U-turn shape via its HMG boxes. Required for maintenance of normal levels of mitochondrial DNA. May play a role in organizing and compacting mitochondrial DNA.

gene.name: transcription factor EB
gene.function: Transcription factor that acts as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, autophagy, lysosomal exocytosis, lipid catabolism, energy metabolism and immune response. Specifically recognizes and binds E-box sequences (5'-CANNTG-3'); efficient DNA-binding requires dimerization with itself or with another MiT/TFE family member such as TFE3 or MITF. Involved in the cellular response to amino acid availability by acting downstream of MTOR: in the presence of nutrients, TFEB phosphorylation by MTOR promotes its cytosolic retention and subsequent inactivation. Upon starvation or lysosomal stress, inhibition of MTOR induces TFEB dephosphorylation, resulting in nuclear localization and transcription factor activity. Specifically recognizes and binds the CLEAR-box sequence (5'-GTCACGTGAC-3') present in the regulatory region of many lysosomal genes, leading to activate their expression, thereby playing a central role in expression of lysosomal genes. Regulates lysosomal positioning in response to nutrient deprivation by promoting the expression of PIP4P1. Acts as a positive regulator of autophagy by promoting expression of genes involved in autophagy. In association with TFE3, activates the expression of CD40L in T-cells, thereby playing a role in T-cell-dependent antibody responses in activated CD4(+) T-cells and thymus-dependent humoral immunity (By similarity). Specifically recognizes the gamma-E3 box, a subset of E-boxes, present in the heavy- chain immunoglobulin enhancer. Plays a role in the signal transduction processes required for normal vascularization of the placenta (By similarity). Involved in the immune response to infection by the bacteria S.aureus, S.typhimurium or S.enterica: infection promotes itaconate production, leading to alkylation, resulting in nuclear localization and transcription factor activity. Itaconate-mediated alkylation activates TFEB- dependent lysosomal biogenesis, facilitating the bacteria clearance during the antibacterial innate immune response. In association with ACSS2, promotes the expression of genes involved in lysosome biogenesis and both autophagy upon glucose deprivation.

gene.name: tyrosine hydroxylase
gene.function: Catalyzes the conversion of L-tyrosine to L- dihydroxyphenylalanine (L-Dopa), the rate-limiting step in the biosynthesis of catecholamines, dopamine, noradrenaline, and adrenaline. Uses tetrahydrobiopterin and molecular oxygen to convert tyrosine to L-Dopa (PubMed:15287903, PubMed:1680128, PubMed:17391063, PubMed:24753243, PubMed:34922205, PubMed:8528210, Ref.18). In addition to tyrosine, is able to catalyze the hydroxylation of phenylalanine and tryptophan with lower specificity (By similarity). Positively regulates the regression of retinal hyaloid vessels during postnatal development (By similarity).

gene.name: tumor necrosis factor
gene.function: Cytokine that binds to TNFRSF1A/TNFR1 and TNFRSF1B/TNFBR. It is mainly secreted by macrophages and can induce cell death of certain tumor cell lines. It is potent pyrogen causing fever by direct action or by stimulation of interleukin-1 secretion and is implicated in the induction of cachexia, Under certain conditions it can stimulate cell proliferation and induce cell differentiation. Impairs regulatory T- cells (Treg) function in individuals with rheumatoid arthritis via FOXP3 dephosphorylation. Up-regulates the expression of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1), which dephosphorylates the key 'Ser-418' residue of FOXP3, thereby inactivating FOXP3 and rendering Treg cells functionally defective. Key mediator of cell death in the anticancer action of BCG-stimulated neutrophils in combination with DIABLO/SMAC mimetic in the RT4v6 bladder cancer cell line. Induces insulin resistance in adipocytes via inhibition of insulin-induced IRS1 tyrosine phosphorylation and insulin-induced glucose uptake. Induces GKAP42 protein degradation in adipocytes which is partially responsible for TNF-induced insulin resistance (By similarity). Plays a role in angiogenesis by inducing VEGF production synergistically with IL1B and IL6. Promotes osteoclastogenesis and therefore mediates bone resorption (By similarity).

gene.name: tyrosinase
gene.function: This is a copper-containing oxidase that functions in the formation of pigments such as melanins and other polyphenolic compounds. Catalyzes the initial and rate limiting step in the cascade of reactions leading to melanin production from tyrosine (By similarity). In addition to hydroxylating tyrosine to DOPA (3,4- dihydroxyphenylalanine), also catalyzes the oxidation of DOPA to DOPA- quinone, and possibly the oxidation of DHI (5,6-dihydroxyindole) to indole-5,6 quinone.

gene.name: VPS33A core subunit of CORVET and HOPS complexes
gene.function: Plays a role in vesicle-mediated protein trafficking to lysosomal compartments including the endocytic membrane transport and autophagic pathways. Believed to act as a core component of the putative HOPS and CORVET endosomal tethering complexes which are proposed to be involved in the Rab5-to-Rab7 endosome conversion probably implicating MON1A/B, and via binding SNAREs and SNARE complexes to mediate tethering and docking events during SNARE-mediated membrane fusion. The HOPS complex is proposed to be recruited to Rab7 on the late endosomal membrane and to regulate late endocytic, phagocytic and autophagic traffic towards lysosomes. The CORVET complex is proposed to function as a Rab5 effector to mediate early endosome fusion probably in specific endosome subpopulations. Required for fusion of endosomes and autophagosomes with lysosomes; the function is dependent on its association with VPS16 but not VIPAS39. The function in autophagosome-lysosome fusion implicates STX17 but not UVRAG.

papers.title: Lysosomal storage diseases.
papers.summary: This review describes Gaucher disease as an autosomal recessive deficiency of glucocerebrosidase that causes glucocerebroside accumulation in reticuloendothelial cells, and outlines its molecular variants, multisystem pathology, and diagnostic approaches. It reports effective systemic treatments with enzyme replacement, eliglustat, miglustat, and bone marrow transplantation, but no proven neurological benefit from enzyme replacement, while highlighting saposin C deficiency as an atypical Gaucher-like mechanism with normal glucocerebrosidase activity.
papers.why: The review reports established enzyme replacement and substrate reduction therapies for Gaucher disease alongside their broader lysosomal-disease development context.

papers.title: Long-term clinical outcomes in type 1 Gaucher disease following 10 years of imiglucerase treatment.
papers.summary: In a retrospective observational cohort of 757 people with type 1 Gaucher disease, 10 years of imiglucerase treatment was associated with sustained improvements in anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, bone pain, and bone crises. The study did not evaluate safety or adverse events and was limited by retrospective registry reporting, incomplete longitudinal data, heterogeneous patients, and potentially inaccurate reporting of skeletal symptoms.
papers.why: The ICGG registry study provides long-term patient data showing that imiglucerase sustainably improves major type 1 Gaucher disease manifestations.

papers.title: Evaluation of miglustat as maintenance therapy after enzyme therapy in adults with stable type 1 Gaucher disease: a prospective, open-label non-inferiority study.
papers.summary: In adults with stable type 1 Gaucher disease previously stabilized by long-term enzyme therapy, 24 months of oral miglustat maintained liver volume and met the prespecified non-inferiority endpoint, while most patients retained therapeutic goals across multiple disease parameters. However, spleen volume, hemoglobin, platelet count, bone marrow infiltration, and chitotriosidase activity worsened in some or most evaluated patients, and gastrointestinal adverse events frequently caused treatment discontinuation.
papers.why: This prospective non-inferiority trial evaluates miglustat as maintenance therapy after enzyme replacement in stable adults with type 1 Gaucher disease.

papers.title: Enzyme replacement therapy for children with acid sphingomyelinase deficiency in the real world: A single center experience in Taiwan.
papers.summary: In two children with chronic neurovisceral acid sphingomyelinase deficiency, one year of olipudase alfa improved several systemic outcomes, including hepatosplenomegaly, liver stiffness, dyslipidemia, interstitial lung disease, growth, walking distance, and lyso-sphingomyelin levels, but did not improve neurocognitive function or peripheral nerve conduction. The paper also discusses shear-wave liver-stiffness assessment as a transferable approach, noting that liver stiffness has been associated with severity and treatment response in Gaucher disease.
papers.why: Real-world olipudase alfa treatment in another lysosomal storage disorder provides transferable evidence for systemic ERT monitoring, including liver stiffness and functional endpoints.

papers.title: Glycosylation and functionality of recombinant β-glucocerebrosidase from various production systems.
papers.summary: This study compared the glycosylation, enzymatic activity, stability, macrophage uptake, and organ biodistribution of three commercial recombinant β-glucocerebrosidase enzyme replacement products for Gaucher disease. Despite substantial glycan-structure differences among taliglucerase alfa, imiglucerase, and velaglucerase alfa, the products had comparable activity, stability, cellular uptake, and broadly similar biodistribution in the tested experimental systems.
papers.why: The study directly compares three approved β-glucocerebrosidase products and validates how production glycosylation affects enzyme activity, macrophage uptake, and tissue distribution.

papers.title: Velaglucerase alfa (VPRIV) enzyme replacement therapy in patients with Gaucher disease: Long-term data from phase III clinical trials.
papers.summary: In 57 patients with type 1 Gaucher disease receiving intravenous velaglucerase alfa for 1.2–4.8 years, treatment improved hematologic measures, spleen and liver volumes, Gaucher disease biomarkers, and adult lumbar-spine bone mineral density; improvements were generally maintained over time. Velaglucerase alfa had favorable long-term tolerability, with no serious adverse event considered related to treatment, although efficacy assessments beyond the primary variables were partly exploratory and longer-term follow-up was incomplete.
papers.why: A long-term extension study provides up to 4.8 years of safety and efficacy data for velaglucerase alfa and identifies responsive clinical and radiographic outcomes in Gaucher disease.

papers.title: A 6-month randomized controlled trial for vitamin E supplementation in pediatric patients with Gaucher disease: Effect on oxidative stress, disease severity and hepatic complications.
papers.summary: This 6-month randomized clinical trial found that pediatric patients with Gaucher disease had increased oxidative stress, with higher malondialdehyde and lower vitamin E and antioxidant enzyme levels than healthy controls. In patients receiving vitamin E alongside stable enzyme replacement therapy, disease severity, liver and spleen volumes, liver stiffness, lyso GL1, and malondialdehyde decreased while antioxidant enzymes increased.
papers.why: A randomized study shows that six months of vitamin E alongside enzyme replacement improves oxidative-stress measures, Gaucher severity, and organ-related outcomes in pediatric Gaucher disease.

papers.title: Mitochondria and quality control defects in a mouse model of Gaucher disease--links to Parkinson's disease.
papers.summary: In a complete gba knockout mouse model of neuronopathic Gaucher disease, the paper shows defective macroautophagy and proteasomal proteostasis, accumulation of p62, ubiquitinated proteins, oligomeric and deposited α-synuclein, and dysfunctional, fragmented mitochondria. MitoQ10 restored mitochondrial membrane potential in cultured gba−/− neurons, while inhibition of Drp1-mediated fission partially restored mitochondrial morphology but not membrane potential, indicating that fragmentation was secondary to bioenergetic dysfunction.
papers.why: The study develops and validates a neuronopathic Gaucher mouse model with cellular quality-control and mitochondrial biomarkers that can be used to test disease mechanisms and therapies.

papers.title: Ambroxol improves lysosomal biochemistry in glucocerebrosidase mutation-linked Parkinson disease cells.
papers.summary: Patient-derived fibroblasts bearing GBA mutations showed reduced glucosylceramidase protein and activity, endoplasmic reticulum retention, oxidative stress, and altered lysosomal biochemistry compared with controls. Ambroxol increased glucosylceramidase expression and activity, reduced oxidative stress and lysosomal stress markers, activated TFEB/CLEAR-network responses, and reduced alpha-synuclein in an overexpressing neuroblastoma model, but did not normalize Gaucher disease enzyme activity to control levels.
papers.why: Ambroxol increased glucocerebrosidase activity and reduced oxidative-stress readouts in fibroblasts from patients with Gaucher disease and GBA1-mutation carriers.

papers.title: Glucocerebrosidase Deficiency in Drosophila Results in α-Synuclein-Independent Protein Aggregation and Neurodegeneration.
papers.summary: The paper establishes a Drosophila dGBA1b deletion model of glucocerebrosidase deficiency that reproduces shortened lifespan, behavioral dysfunction, neurodegeneration, memory impairment, and excessive ubiquitinated-protein aggregation. Loss of dGBA1b is associated with defective autophagic/lysosomal protein turnover largely independent of α-synuclein, although glucocerebrosidase deficiency mildly enhances α-synuclein aggregation and dopaminergic-neuron toxicity.
papers.why: The paper develops and characterizes a GBA1-deficient fly model with lifespan, locomotor, memory, aggregate, and neurodegenerative phenotypes.

papers.title: Ambroxol effects in glucocerebrosidase and α-synuclein transgenic mice.
papers.summary: In mice, oral ambroxol increased brain glucocerebrosidase activity in wild-type, heterozygous Gba1-L444P knock-in, and human α-synuclein-overexpressing models, with the largest rescue in the lysosomal fraction of L444P/+ brain. In α-synuclein-overexpressing mice it also reduced α-synuclein and, in some regions, S129-phosphorylated α-synuclein, but it did not increase GCase mRNA or alter TFEB/TFAM protein levels, supporting a post-transcriptional chaperone mechanism while leaving clinical efficacy in Gaucher or Parkinson disease unproven.
papers.why: Ambroxol increased brain glucocerebrosidase activity in multiple GBA-related mouse models and reduced α-synuclein species in α-synuclein-overexpressing mice.

papers.title: Glucosylsphingosine is a highly sensitive and specific biomarker for primary diagnostic and follow-up monitoring in Gaucher disease in a non-Jewish, Caucasian cohort of Gaucher disease patients.
papers.summary: In a observational cohort study, plasma glucosylsphingosine measured by HPLC-MS/MS distinguished Gaucher disease patients from healthy controls, carriers, and patients with other lysosomal storage diseases at a 12 ng/ml cutoff, with reported sensitivity and specificity of 100%. Glucosylsphingosine also decreased during enzyme replacement therapy, with levels associated with GBA1 variants, although its relationship with clinical outcomes and optimal monitoring use requires further validation.
papers.why: Patient and control data show that glucosylsphingosine is sensitive and specific for Gaucher disease and declines during treatment, supporting diagnosis and follow-up monitoring.

papers.title: Ambroxol chaperone therapy for neuronopathic Gaucher disease: A pilot study.
papers.summary: In an uncontrolled pilot study of five patients with neuronopathic Gaucher disease, high-dose oral ambroxol combined with enzyme replacement therapy increased lymphocyte glucocerebrosidase activity, reduced cerebrospinal-fluid glucosylsphingosine, and was associated with improvement of myoclonus, selected seizure outcomes, pupillary light-reflex function, and motor function. Dystonia did not improve, seizure responses were mixed, and efficacy remains uncertain because the cohort was very small, lacked a randomized control group, and had heterogeneous disease and follow-up.
papers.why: A pilot study in neuronopathic Gaucher disease showed that ambroxol increased glucocerebrosidase activity, reduced CSF glucosylsphingosine, and improved several neurological outcomes.

papers.title: Pilot study of newborn screening for six lysosomal storage diseases using Tandem Mass Spectrometry.
papers.summary: A pilot study showed that a 6-plex tandem mass spectrometry newborn-screening assay can measure glucocerebrosidase activity in dried blood spots and identify newborns at risk for Gaucher disease. Among approximately 43,000 newborns, three samples were screen-positive; sequencing found one with a normal GBA sequence, one heterozygous carrier of p.N370S, and one probably affected with Gaucher disease type I.
papers.why: The study validates a high-throughput tandem-MS newborn-screening assay that measures glucocerebrosidase activity and confirms suspected Gaucher disease by sequencing.

papers.title: Hyposmia and cognitive impairment in Gaucher disease patients and carriers.
papers.summary: In an observational cohort, Type I Gaucher disease patients and heterozygous GBA mutation carriers had poorer olfaction and cognition and more parkinsonian motor signs than matched controls. The findings may identify a clinical prodromal phenotype associated with later neurodegeneration, but the markers lacked specificity, and no group differences were found for rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder or autonomic dysfunction.
papers.why: The cohort study applies standardized olfactory, cognitive, motor, sleep, and autonomic measures to Gaucher patients and carriers, providing usable outcome measures.

papers.title: Timing of initiation of enzyme replacement therapy after diagnosis of type 1 Gaucher disease: effect on incidence of avascular necrosis.
papers.summary: In a retrospective analysis of 2,700 International Collaborative Gaucher Group registry patients with type 1 Gaucher disease, initiation of imiglucerase within 2 years of diagnosis was associated with a 41% lower adjusted incidence of new-onset avascular necrosis than later initiation. Prior splenectomy was associated with more than twice the avascular necrosis risk, but the nonrandomized design, heterogeneous treated population, and lack of an untreated comparator prevent attributing these associations definitively to treatment timing.
papers.why: Registry data from 2,700 treated patients show that earlier ERT initiation is associated with lower avascular-necrosis incidence.

papers.title: Evaluation of the detection of GBA missense mutations and other variants using the Oxford Nanopore MinION.
papers.summary: The study validates a long-read Oxford Nanopore MinION laboratory and bioinformatic protocol for detecting, phasing, and analyzing coding, intronic, and structural GBA variants in samples that included patients with Gaucher disease. The method detected all known missense variants and a 55-bp deletion at correct zygosity, while one RecNciI recombinant allele was missed because long-range PCR failed to amplify it.
papers.why: Validates a long-read sequencing workflow that detects and phases GBA1 variants in Gaucher and Parkinson samples, directly accelerating mutation detection and genetic analysis.

papers.title: Immunoglobulin and free light chain abnormalities in Gaucher disease type I: data from an adult cohort of 63 patients and review of the literature.
papers.summary: This study found frequent polyclonal gammopathy (41%) and MGUS (19%) in an adult Gaucher disease type I cohort, with MGUS prevalence increasing with age but not tracking disease severity or treatment exposure. Serum free-light-chain measurements did not reliably predict MGUS or multiple myeloma, whereas strongly abnormal κ/λ ratios identified the few patients with impending or existing myeloma/amyloidosis; enzyme replacement therapy showed a possible benefit for immunoglobulin abnormalities, but the authors emphasized the need for larger confirmatory studies.
papers.why: Quantifies immunoglobulin abnormalities and evaluates free light chains as candidate MGUS/myeloma biomarkers in a 63-patient Gaucher cohort.

papers.title: Outcomes after 18 months of eliglustat therapy in treatment-naïve adults with Gaucher disease type 1: The phase 3 ENGAGE trial.
papers.summary: In treatment-naïve adults with Gaucher disease type 1, eliglustat improved visceral, hematologic, skeletal, and biochemical disease measures over 18 months, while reducing glucosylsphingosine and other biomarkers. Treatment was generally well tolerated, with no new long-term safety concerns, although two serious atrioventricular block episodes were considered probably related in one asymptomatic patient.
papers.why: The ENGAGE trial provides direct clinical evidence that eliglustat improves visceral, hematologic, skeletal, and biochemical disease measures over 18 months.

papers.title: Elevation of glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B in type 1 Gaucher disease patients and mouse models.
papers.summary: The paper identifies glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B (gpNMB) as a biomarker produced by glucosylceramide-laden Gaucher cells, with markedly elevated levels in plasma and tissues of humans and mice with Gaucher disease. Plasma gpNMB tracks other Gaucher-cell markers and decreases after enzyme replacement therapy, eliglustat-mediated substrate reduction, or GBA gene therapy, although it does not measure disease severity or independently support primary diagnosis.
papers.why: The study identifies gpNMB as a treatment-responsive Gaucher-cell marker and shows that gene transfer or substrate reduction normalizes it.

papers.title: Systemic delivery of a glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor reduces CNS substrates and increases lifespan in a mouse model of type 2 Gaucher disease.
papers.summary: Systemic administration of GZ 161 to K14 mice reduced brain glucosylceramide and glucosylsphingosine, attenuated macrophage/microglial and astrocytic pathology, and increased median lifespan. Combining GZ 161 with intracerebroventricular recombinant human glucocerebrosidase produced an additive survival benefit, but substrate normalization and full CNS rescue were not achieved.
papers.why: Demonstrates that a systemic glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor crosses the blood-brain barrier, reduces CNS substrates and pathology, and extends lifespan in a type 2 Gaucher mouse model.

papers.title: Impaired autophagic and mitochondrial functions are partially restored by ERT in Gaucher and Fabry diseases.
papers.summary: In patient-derived peripheral blood mononuclear cells, Gaucher disease is associated with lysosomal accumulation, impaired basal autophagy, disrupted mTOR responsiveness, and altered mitochondrial regulation; many of these abnormalities are shared with Fabry disease. Recombinant glucocerebrosidase/enzyme replacement therapy partially normalizes LAMP1, LC3, Tfam, mitochondrial DNA copy number, and some ATP or mitochondrial activity measures, but effects on autophagosome formation, lysosome volume, and ATP are inconsistent across Gaucher subtypes and experimental contexts.
papers.why: The study directly shows partial restoration of autophagic, lysosomal, and mitochondrial abnormalities in Gaucher patient PBMCs after ERT and identifies measurable pathway markers.

papers.title: Identification of a biomarker in cerebrospinal fluid for neuronopathic forms of Gaucher disease.
papers.summary: This paper identifies GPNMB in cerebrospinal fluid as a biomarker that is elevated in neuronopathic Gaucher disease and correlates with clinical severity and neuropathology in patients and mouse models. Proteomics, ELISA, and Western blotting independently validate the elevation, while CSF GPNMB also changes with disease progression and cessation of experimental GlcCerase inhibition in mice.
papers.why: The study identifies CSF GPNMB as a validated-in-model marker that tracks neuropathology and symptom severity in neuronopathic Gaucher disease.

papers.title: The definition of neuronopathic Gaucher disease.
papers.summary: This consensus paper defines neuronopathic Gaucher disease by the coexistence of acid β-glucosidase deficiency, bi-allelic pathogenic GBA1 variants, and gaze palsy, and distinguishes the acute GD2 form from the subacute or chronic GD3 form. It also identifies clinical, genetic, and electrophysiological features that support, distinguish, or exclude neuronopathic Gaucher disease.
papers.why: The consensus definition provides a directly reusable diagnostic framework for distinguishing neuronopathic Gaucher subtypes and recruiting appropriate patients for trials.

papers.title: LC-MS/MS multiplex analysis of lysosphingolipids in plasma and amniotic fluid: A novel tool for the screening of sphingolipidoses and Niemann-Pick type C disease.
papers.summary: The study developed a multiplex LC-MS/MS assay for lysosphingolipids and validated it in plasma and amniotic fluid. Lysohexosylceramide was highly elevated in plasma and amniotic fluid from Gaucher disease patients or affected fetuses and provided a sensitive screening approach, although diagnosis still required confirmatory enzymatic or genetic testing.
papers.why: The validated multiplex assay sensitively and specifically detects Gaucher disease in plasma and identifies elevated lysohexosylceramide in affected amniotic fluid.

papers.title: Outcomes after 8 years of eliglustat therapy for Gaucher disease type 1: Final results from the Phase 2 trial.
papers.summary: In an uncontrolled 8-year Phase 2 study of 19 completers, eliglustat produced sustained improvements in visceral, hematologic, skeletal, quality-of-life, disease-severity, and Gaucher disease biomarker outcomes in previously untreated adults with Gaucher disease type 1. Substrate biomarkers fell substantially, and treatment was generally well tolerated, although the small open-label study lacked a comparator and included patients with intact spleens and relatively mild skeletal involvement.
papers.why: This long-term phase 2 study demonstrates sustained clinical and biochemical responses to eliglustat in previously untreated type 1 Gaucher disease.

papers.title: Biochemical response to substrate reduction therapy versus enzyme replacement therapy in Gaucher disease type 1 patients.
papers.summary: In this small retrospective series, eliglustat and enzyme replacement therapy produced comparable reductions in biochemical markers and similar short-term clinical responses in treatment-naïve patients with Gaucher disease type 1. Miglustat produced smaller biochemical responses, frequent deterioration after switching from enzyme replacement therapy, and several discontinuations because of adverse events or treatment failure.
papers.why: The study evaluates biochemical markers and clinical measures to compare eliglustat, miglustat, and enzyme replacement therapy in type 1 Gaucher disease.

papers.title: Newborn screening for Morquio disease and other lysosomal storage diseases: results from the 8-plex assay for 70,000 newborns.
papers.summary: The study reports a prospective newborn screening program using an 8-plex tandem mass spectrometry assay that includes Gaucher disease, alongside Pompe disease, Fabry disease, MPS I, MPS II, MPS 3B, MPS 4A, and MPS 6. One newborn was identified with Gaucher disease, had elevated plasma glucosylsphingosine (LysoGb1), and began treatment at 41 days of age because of thrombocytopenia; the paper does not specify the treatment used.
papers.why: The 70,000-newborn study demonstrates an MS/MS screening workflow that detected Gaucher disease and enabled treatment beginning at 41 days of age.

papers.title: Demographics and patient characteristics of 1209 patients with Gaucher disease: Descriptive analysis from the Gaucher Outcome Survey (GOS).
papers.summary: The Gaucher Outcome Survey provides real-world baseline data for 1,209 patients with Gaucher disease, showing predominance of type 1 disease, the N370S/N370S genotype, treatment exposure, and variable visceral and skeletal manifestations. The paper identifies GBA1-related β-glucocerebrosidase deficiency and lysosomal glucocerebroside accumulation as disease mechanisms and describes several enzyme replacement therapies, substrate reduction therapies, diagnostic approaches, and longitudinal outcome measures that can support Gaucher disease research and management.
papers.why: The international GOS is an existing longitudinal registry of 1,209 patients designed to assess Gaucher treatment outcomes, safety, and disease characteristics.

papers.title: The heat shock protein amplifier arimoclomol improves refolding, maturation and lysosomal activity of glucocerebrosidase.
papers.summary: Arimoclomol amplified HSP70-family chaperones and improved folding, maturation, lysosomal localization, and residual activity of mutant GCase across major Gaucher disease genotypes in patient-derived fibroblasts and a human MASC-derived neuronal model. These in vitro findings provide preclinical proof of concept for arimoclomol in neuronopathic Gaucher disease, but clinical efficacy and CNS benefit were not established.
papers.why: Arimoclomol enhanced folding, maturation, lysosomal localization, and activity of mutant GCase in GD patient fibroblasts and a patient-derived neuronal model.

papers.title: The saccadic and neurological deficits in type 3 Gaucher disease.
papers.summary: In a prospective 2–4-year observational study of 15 patients with type 3 Gaucher disease, scleral-search-coil measurements showed abnormal and direction-dependent saccades, with horizontal and downward saccades generally more impaired than vertical and upward saccades. Saccadic measures and the Purdue Pegboard test were proposed as objective neurological outcome measures, while long-term stability and inconsistent decline limited their demonstrated sensitivity to progression.
papers.why: Prospective four-year data establish saccadic measurements and oculo-manual dexterity as longitudinal neurological outcome measures and potential therapeutic-trial endpoints in type 3 Gaucher disease.

papers.title: Skeletal improvement in patients with Gaucher disease type 1: a phase 2 trial of oral eliglustat.
papers.summary: In an open-label phase 2 trial, four years of oral eliglustat in 19 adults with Gaucher disease type 1 was associated with improved femoral marrow infiltration and increased lumbar spine bone mineral density, while cortical thickness and most focal lesions remained unchanged. Fractures and bone crises were not observed, but the small uncontrolled study, unblinded image reviews, variable skeletal responses, and isolated adverse or indeterminate findings limit causal conclusions.
papers.why: A four-year phase 2 trial provides direct evidence that oral eliglustat can improve skeletal manifestations of Gaucher disease type 1.

papers.title: Pharmacologic properties of high-dose ambroxol in four patients with Gaucher disease and myoclonic epilepsy.
papers.summary: In four patients with neuronopathic Gaucher disease, combined high-dose ambroxol and enzyme replacement therapy increased residual glucocerebrosidase activity and reduced plasma and dried-blood-spot Lyso-Gb1 levels. Neurological outcomes initially worsened or remained impaired, but seizures, disease severity, and daily-function scores improved after ambroxol was escalated to 27 mg/kg/day; treatment was generally tolerable, although mucus-related respiratory difficulty and drug interactions were observed.
papers.why: Long-term patient data show that high-dose ambroxol plus ERT enhanced residual GCase activity, normalized Lyso-Gb1, and improved seizures and neurocognition at the highest dose.

papers.title: Dysregulation of mitochondria-lysosome contacts by GBA1 dysfunction in dopaminergic neuronal models of Parkinson's disease.
papers.summary: In GBA1-mutant, Parkinson’s disease patient-derived midbrain dopaminergic neurons, reduced GCase activity, glucosylceramide accumulation, reduced TBC1D15, and impaired Rab7 hydrolysis produced prolonged mitochondria–lysosome contacts, axonal mitochondrial depletion, reduced respiration, and lower ATP. S-181 restored GCase-related contact dynamics, while TBC1D15 expression partially rescued downstream mitochondrial defects; the paper did not study Gaucher disease or use Gaucher patient-derived models.
papers.why: The paper provides experimental rescue approaches in human GBA1-mutant neuronal models and demonstrates rescue by increasing GCase activity.

papers.title: The emerging role of autophagic-lysosomal dysfunction in Gaucher disease and Parkinson's disease.
papers.summary: This review reports that GBA1/GCase deficiency is associated with lysosomal-autophagic dysfunction, altered mTORC1 signaling, α-synuclein accumulation, and neurodegeneration in Gaucher disease models. Rapamycin rescued lifespan, locomotor, and oxidative-stress phenotypes in GCase-deficient flies, but cited evidence also shows cell death in GBA1-mutant GD iPSC-derived neurons, making transfer uncertain and model-dependent.
papers.why: The paper reports functional rescue of lifespan, locomotor, and oxidative-stress phenotypes in a GCase-deficient fly model using the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin.

papers.title: Targeting neuronal lysosomal dysfunction caused by β-glucocerebrosidase deficiency with an enzyme-based brain shuttle construct.
papers.summary: The study develops GCase-BS, a transferrin-receptor-targeted fusion of β-glucocerebrosidase, and shows improved neuronal uptake, lysosomal delivery, and hydrolysis of glucosylsphingosine and glucosylceramide in GBA-deficient cellular systems. In neuronopathic Gaucher disease mouse models, intravenous GCase-BS crosses the blood-brain barrier, reduces brain lipids, and lowers plasma neurofilament light, but rapid blood clearance, limited dose response, and dependence on the composite 4 L/PS-NA genotype remain important limitations.
papers.why: This study develops and tests a blood-brain barrier penetrant glucocerebrosidase construct that improves enzyme uptake, reduces disease-related lipids, and rescues lysosomal abnormalities in Gaucher-relevant models.

papers.title: Patient centered guidelines for the laboratory diagnosis of Gaucher disease type 1.
papers.summary: This guideline synthesizes evidence and recommends a diagnostic workflow for Gaucher disease type 1 using first-line biomarkers, beta-glucocerebrosidase activity testing, and GBA1 molecular analysis. It emphasizes confirmation with leukocyte or cultured fibroblast enzyme assays and GBA1 testing because biomarker specificity, dried-blood-spot predictive value, and interpretation of uncertain sequence variants are limited.
papers.why: This guideline offers standardized, disease-specific biochemical, genetic, and algorithmic approaches for timely and accurate Gaucher disease diagnosis.

papers.title: Substrate compositional variation with tissue/region and Gba1 mutations in mouse models--implications for Gaucher disease.
papers.summary: In Gba1 mutant mouse models, the tissue distribution and composition of glucosylceramide and glucosylsphingosine depended strongly on mutation, residual acid β-glucosidase activity, tissue, and age. Saposin C deficiency lowered GCase activity and exposed mutation-specific substrate preferences, including D409V-associated visceral accumulation and V394L/D409H-associated brain defects.
papers.why: The work characterizes substrate accumulation in multiple Gba1 mouse models and establishes mutation-, tissue-, and age-specific biochemical measures relevant to Gaucher disease modeling.

papers.title: Immunogenicity of glycans on biotherapeutic drugs produced in plant expression systems-The taliglucerase alfa story.
papers.summary: Taliglucerase alfa was generally safe and effective in Gaucher disease patients, while a validated competitive ELISA found that anti-plant glycan antibodies were uncommon and were not associated with impaired efficacy or increased treatment-related adverse events. The study found no evidence that the plant-derived glycans on taliglucerase alfa posed a greater immunogenicity risk than mammalian-cell-derived enzyme replacement therapies.
papers.why: The study developed and validated an assay for detecting plant-specific glycan antibodies and used it to assess immunogenicity and clinical relevance in taliglucerase alfa-treated Gaucher patients.

papers.title: Upregulation of proinflammatory cytokines in the fetal brain of the Gaucher mouse.
papers.summary: In a glucocerebrosidase-knockout mouse model of Gaucher disease, the paper found increased proinflammatory cytokine expression, nitric oxide production, and region-specific microglial reactive oxygen species. Conduritol B epoxide-treated primary microglia reproduced selected inflammatory changes, but the study could not establish that cytokines, nitric oxide, or reactive oxygen species directly cause neurodegenerative symptoms.
papers.why: The Gaucher mouse study identifies inflammatory cytokine, nitric oxide, and reactive oxygen species changes in the brain, providing disease-relevant biomarkers and mechanistic model evidence.

papers.title: Venglustat combined with imiglucerase for neurological disease in adults with Gaucher disease type 3: the LEAP trial.
papers.summary: In an open-label Phase 2 trial, once-daily venglustat added to imiglucesterase reduced plasma and cerebrospinal fluid glucosylceramide and glucosylsphingosine in most adults with Gaucher disease type 3, demonstrating brain target engagement. Treatment was generally tolerable and accompanied by modest ataxia improvement and exploratory MRI signals, but adaptive function deteriorated, saccades did not improve, responses were inconsistent in one patient with low exposure, and efficacy remains unconfirmed because the study was small and uncontrolled.
papers.why: The LEAP trial directly tested venglustat with imiglucerase in Gaucher type 3 and reported pharmacokinetic, biochemical, MRI, and neurologic outcomes.

papers.title: Eliglustat tartrate for the treatment of adults with type 1 Gaucher disease.
papers.summary: This review reports that eliglustat tartrate is a CYP2D6-dependent, oral substrate reduction therapy that inhibits glucosylceramide synthase, lowers glucosylceramide burden, and improves hematologic, visceral, skeletal, and biomarker outcomes in adults with Gaucher disease type 1. It also summarizes GBA1 enzyme activity as the diagnostic gold standard, chitotriosidase and PARC/CCL18 as monitoring biomarkers, and glucosylsphingosine as a potentially more sensitive and specific diagnostic marker.
papers.why: The review summarizes approved eliglustat therapy, its molecular mechanism, dosing strategy, and clinical development for type 1 Gaucher disease.

papers.title: Transformation in pretreatment manifestations of Gaucher disease type 1 during two decades of alglucerase/imiglucerase enzyme replacement therapy in the International Collaborative Gaucher Group (ICGG) Gaucher Registry.
papers.summary: In 1,427 US patients with Gaucher disease type 1 initiating alglucerase/imiglucerase, later treatment eras were associated with markedly less pretreatment splenectomy and fewer destructive bone events, especially in pediatric patients and adults younger than 50 years. The paper also describes enzyme replacement therapy as established care for Gaucher disease and links timely treatment to prevention of splenectomy and skeletal complications, while bone pain and pretreatment hematologic measures showed little temporal improvement.
papers.why: The registry analysis demonstrates two decades of real-world alglucerase/imiglucerase treatment effects and provides clinically relevant outcome measures for GD1 management.

papers.title: Clinical outcomes after 4.5 years of eliglustat therapy for Gaucher disease type 1: Phase 3 ENGAGE trial final results.
papers.summary: The Phase 3 ENGAGE trial found that up to 4.5 years of eliglustat in previously untreated adults with Gaucher disease type 1 improved splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, bone mineral density, Gaucher cell biomarkers, and accumulating sphingolipids. The therapy was generally well tolerated, although persistent thrombocytopenia and anemia occurred in subsets of patients, and bone marrow burden improvement was modest without an established clinically significant threshold.
papers.why: Final phase 3 ENGAGE results show sustained clinical and biochemical improvement with eliglustat over 4.5 years in previously untreated type 1 Gaucher disease.

papers.title: C5a Activates a Pro-Inflammatory Gene Expression Profile in Human Gaucher iPSC-Derived Macrophages.
papers.summary: Human type 2 Gaucher disease iPSC-derived macrophages showed an exaggerated C5a-triggered inflammatory response, including approximately sixfold greater sensitivity in TNF-α mRNA induction and 8–10-fold higher TNF-α secretion than C5a-stimulated controls. PMX53-mediated C5aR1 blockade and recombinant GCase both prevented excess TNF-α secretion, supporting the C5a-C5aR1 axis and GCase deficiency as mechanistic and therapeutic targets, although conclusions require validation in additional patient lines.
papers.why: The paper validates Gaucher iPSC-derived macrophages as a disease model and provides experimental evidence that C5aR1 inhibition with PMX53 reverses heightened inflammatory cytokine production.

papers.title: Long-term adverse event profile from four completed trials of oral eliglustat in adults with Gaucher disease type 1.
papers.summary: Pooled long-term data from 393 adults with Gaucher disease type 1 showed that eliglustat had a generally favorable safety profile over a mean 3.6 years, with most treatment-related adverse events being mild or moderate and generally occurring once. Adverse events declined over time, did not increase with dose, and were not accompanied by clinically significant QTcF prolongation at the observed therapeutic eliglustat concentrations.
papers.why: The pooled analysis of 393 adults with type 1 Gaucher disease provides long-term eliglustat exposure and adverse-event data useful for clinical treatment planning.

papers.title: Interstitial lung disease in lysosomal storage disorders.
papers.summary: This review finds that pulmonary involvement is an uncommon but clinically important manifestation of Gaucher disease, driven by Gaucher-cell infiltration of pulmonary compartments and associated with restrictive impairment, reduced diffusion capacity, pulmonary hypertension, and rare interstitial lung disease. Enzyme replacement therapy reverses haematological and visceral manifestations and has improved hepatopulmonary syndrome in an isolated case, but has rarely alleviated Gaucher-associated interstitial lung disease; lung transplantation has been used in severe cases.
papers.why: The review reports Gaucher-specific pulmonary assessment methods and evidence that timely ERT can prevent pulmonary and other organ failure.

papers.title: Comparative therapeutic effects of velaglucerase alfa and imiglucerase in a Gaucher disease mouse model.
papers.summary: In a D409V/null mouse model of Gaucher disease, weekly intravenous velaglucerase alfa and imiglucerase produced broadly similar dose- and time-dependent reductions in hepatic and splenic glucosylceramide and storage cells. Velaglucerase alfa reduced hepatic glucosylceramide more than imiglucerase at 4 weeks with 60 U/kg, but the difference disappeared by 8 weeks; neither therapy appreciably cleared pulmonary storage, and both generated potentially serious anti-GCase immune responses.
papers.why: The paper directly compares two GCase replacement therapies in a Gaucher mouse model using pharmacokinetic, tissue distribution, biomarker, efficacy, and immunogenicity endpoints.

papers.title: Cancer risk and gammopathies in 2123 adults with Gaucher disease type 1 in the International Gaucher Group Gaucher Registry.
papers.summary: In a large international observational registry of 2,123 adults with Gaucher disease type 1, malignancy, MGUS, and polyclonal gammopathy risks were higher than in the general US population for several cancers, while progression from MGUS to multiple myeloma was comparable to the general population. The paper identifies lysosomal lipid accumulation, tissue macrophage dysfunction, chronic metabolic inflammation, and B-cell activation as a potential cancer-permissive mechanism and recommends longitudinal surveillance, while noting that treatment effects on gammopathy and malignancy require further study.
papers.why: The large Gaucher disease registry provides longitudinal natural-history data and monitoring outcomes for hematologic malignancies, MGUS and solid tumors.

papers.title: Specific saposin C deficiency: CNS impairment and acid beta-glucosidase effects in the mouse.
papers.summary: This study shows that selective saposin C deficiency in mice causes a slowly progressive Gaucher-like neurological phenotype, with reduced GCase activity, mild tissue-specific glycosphingolipid accumulation, cerebellar Purkinje-cell and granule-cell loss, axonal pathology, inflammation, and impaired hippocampal long-term potentiation. The findings indicate that saposin C supports CNS and axonal integrity through roles partly independent of its enhancement and stabilization of GCase.
papers.why: This knock-in mouse model reproduces saposin C-deficiency CNS disease and provides a platform for studying GCase-associated glycosphingolipid accumulation and neurological phenotypes.
